Urmila: Fifteen replies, and the same line in every one. "Come back when there are customers."
Ritu: I know. I've read them again and again.
Urmila: So what are they telling us?
Ritu: That the deck isn't the problem. I've been fixing slides when I should have been finding customers.
Urmila: Then no more pitching until that changes.
Ritu: Agreed. I'll call the three clinics that tried the demo and ask if they'd sign a pilot.
Urmila: And if one says no?
Ritu: Then I ask what would make it a yes.
A month later, in the same room:
Ritu: Three pilots signed. Ready to send the new deck.
Urmila: Send it to the ones who wrote "customers".

By the fifteenth no, I could recite the email: "Interesting product, but we'd like to see more traction." Fifteen investors, one concern. I kept thinking the next meeting would be different. Finally Lakshmi, my co-founder, said, "Vijay, they're all telling us the same thing. Why are we still pitching?"
So we stopped. We cancelled the four meetings on the calendar and spent seven weeks on nothing but getting pilot customers for our warehouse-tracking tool. Lakshmi visited every logistics park near Chakan. I rewrote the setup so a warehouse could start in a day. We signed three pilots: small, but paying.
Then we went back. Not to new investors, but to the ones who had said no. The deck opened with the three pilots and their results. Two of the fifteen asked for a second meeting within a week.

qa.q: How many pilots did they sign?
What was Vijay feeling before Lakshmi's question?
qa.a: Vijay kept hoping the next meeting would be different, feeling stubborn and a little stuck.

qa.q: Why was going back to the same investors smart?
qa.a: They had already named traction as their one concern, so three paying pilots answered it directly.

qa.q: How might the investors who asked for a second meeting see the new deck?
qa.a: They would likely feel their concern was taken seriously and be more confident in the team.

grounding: It shows a founder, after fifteen rejections over the same concern, pausing the pitching, signing three pilot customers and returning to investors with better evidence.

Incubator mentor's note, 20 June.
Siddharth came in today and put a list on my desk: fifteen investor rejections since February, and in thirteen of them the same sentence about "not enough proof that hospitals will pay". He had been treating each no as bad luck. Today, for the first time, he read them together.
He said, "I've been fixing the slides. They're telling me to fix the business." He has decided to pause all investor meetings for two months and use the time to sign pilot customers.
I introduced him to two hospital administrators from our network. He will visit both next week.
Update, 2 September: Siddharth has three signed pilots, two of them paid. He has rewritten the deck to open with them and is going back to four of the investors who said no.
— Gargi

qa.q: In how many rejections did the same sentence appear?
How might Siddharth have felt reading the rejections together?
qa.a: He likely felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, seeing that the investors wanted the business fixed, not the slides.

qa.q: What else did the mentor do to help?
qa.a: Introduced him to two hospital administrators, turning his plan into real visits.

qa.q: How does Gargi see the change by September?
qa.a: Gargi sees solid progress: three signed pilots, a rewritten deck and a return to investors with evidence.

grounding: It shows a founder noticing that repeated rejections share one concern, pausing pitches to sign pilot customers and returning to investors with evidence.
